archetype.name: Retooling (out-shot, under-finishing)
archetype.definition: A year after a playoff season, Philadelphia is leaning on young forwards and a reshuffled blueline, and right now it is losing the 5-on-5 game badly while its goalies and penalty kill keep the scores closer than the play.

report.headline: Bad record, worse 5-on-5 play; the goalies are hiding how lopsided it is
report.take:
The Flyers are 4-10-5, 30th of 32 on the site, and last in the Metropolitan. Unlike many bad starts, this one is not a story of bad bounces in close games. Their Pts vs Goal Diff is -0.3, essentially neutral, so the standings reflect the goals. The goals reflect the play: a 41.5% xGF share and 45% CF share, both near the bottom of the league, 24.1 shots a game (30th) against 28.9 allowed (26th). This is a team that spends too much of its night defending.

The drop from last year is the real headline. The 2025-26 club went 43-27-12, won four playoff games and controlled 50.6% of expected goals. The two seasons before that also had above-50% xGF shares and were sunk by goaltending, with GSAx of -19.9 and -45.8. This year the pattern has flipped. The goalies are 3.5 goals above expected, 10th in the league, with Joseph Woll at +3.6. The skaters are the problem. Trevor Zegras leads the forwards in ice time and points (14) but sits at a 36.3% xGF. Only Denver Barkey (56.2%) and Noah Cates (51.1%) are above water among the regular forwards, and the defense grades D- with Cam York at -10 and a tab rank of 235th of 252.

The numbers do hide one thing: the finishing is unusually cold. Skaters are shooting 9.2% against a league mark of 11.6%, and the 5-on-5 PDO is 97.4, so some scoring should come back. But Matvei Michkov's 10 goals on 27 shots are already doing a lot of the lifting, and that rate won't hold. The rest of the forward group has to warm up just for the offense to stay level. The opening nine-game losing streak also inflates the season-long damage. Over the last 10 the Flyers went 4-4-2 with a -1 differential and 3.1 goals a game, a team that loses one-goal games rather than gets blown out.

Where this goes depends on whether the shot share recovers toward last year's level. Without that, warmer shooting and solid goaltending can lift them from historically bad to merely bad: out of the playoff picture well before spring, with the season's value measured in how Michkov, Martone, Barkey and Bonk develop.

strengths.title: Goaltending above expected
strengths.body: The team's goalies have saved 3.5 goals more than an average goalie would on these shots, 10th in the league and a sharp reversal from the -45.8 of two seasons ago. Joseph Woll carries it at +3.6 with a .899 save %, while Dan Vladar is slightly below expected. The raw save % is only middling because the shot load is heavy. Woll's level looks sustainable enough to keep games close, and he should get the bigger share of starts.

strengths.title: A penalty kill that holds
strengths.body: The PK is killing 80.6% of penalties, 10th in the league and well above the league average, and better than last season's 77.6%. With a team this often on its heels, the kill keeps special teams from widening the hole. Combined with the goaltending, it is a big part of why the goal differential isn't even worse than the underlying shot share suggests.

strengths.title: Competitive since the opening skid
strengths.body: After opening with a nine-game losing streak, the Flyers have gone 4-4-2 over their last 10 with a -1 differential, scoring 3.1 a game. That is more than a goal a game better than their full-season differential. Two of the recent losses came in overtime. This is closer to their true level than the season line, though the last five (1-3-1) show it is a sub-.500 team, not a turned corner.

concerns.title: Losing the 5-on-5 game badly
concerns.body: A 41.5% xGF share ranks 30th, down from 50.6% last season, and the Flyers are well behind on attempts and shots both ways. This is structural rather than bad luck, and it runs through the top of the lineup: Zegras (36.3%) and Dvorak (39.8%) take the most center minutes and are getting outplayed. Until this moves, the ceiling stays low no matter how the goalies play.

concerns.title: A blueline that leaks and can't drive play
concerns.body: The defense grades D-, and no regular defenseman is above a 47% xGF share. Sanheim plays 25 minutes a night at 43.9%, Drysdale 23 minutes at 38.5%, and York has been a -10 in 11 games. Opposing defensemen produce 0.40 points a game more than their norms against Philadelphia, 30th in the league. That points to a group that loses the puck battles that let opposing blueliners activate.

concerns.title: Offense too thin to absorb regression
concerns.body: At 2.21 goals a game, 31st, the Flyers sit nearly a goal below the league average. Team shooting is cold at 9.2%, so some scoring should return. But Michkov's 10 goals on 27 shots will cool, and the power play remains poor at 17.2% (27th), extending a multi-year weakness. Low shot volume limits how much a shooting rebound can help.

trend.note: A nine-game skid to open, a three-game win streak in mid-October, then a 1-3-1 last five. Outside the opening hole, this has been a consistent sub-.500 team that keeps games close and loses more than it wins.

weekAhead.headline: A soft Vancouver opener, then Edmonton twice around Columbus
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Vancouver against the only team ranked below the Flyers: 3-15-1, with the league's worst defense, an .859 save %, a -14.6 GSAx and a 63.5% penalty kill. That is exactly the opponent where a cold-shooting team with a weak power play can find goals. Anything short of a win there is a bad sign. The Columbus road game is a fair fight between two low-scoring teams; the Blue Jackets rank 29th in offense and beat the Flyers 4-3 in overtime last month.

The two Edmonton games are the hard part. The Oilers are 12-3-3 with the league's top offense and a 33.8% power play, though that scoring rides a league-best 16% shooting and an all-situations PDO of 105.4. Their 49.1% xGF share is ordinary, yet still well ahead of Philadelphia's. Two or three wins from the four would be a decent week.

keyMatchups.title: Cold Flyers shooters vs Vancouver's goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Vancouver's goalies have a league-worst .859 save % and the Canucks allow 31 shots a game, 31st. They also concede 2.44 points a game to forwards above expectation, the worst mark in the league. If Philadelphia's 9.2% shooting is going to turn, this is the night.

keyMatchups.title: Edmonton's power play vs Flyers' kill
keyMatchups.body: The Oilers convert 33.8% of their power plays, third in the league, against a Flyers kill that ranks 10th. Philadelphia can't afford to give Edmonton's finishers extra chances on top of the 5-on-5 deficit. Discipline decides whether these two games stay close.

keyMatchups.title: Woll's starts in the hard games
keyMatchups.body: Woll is 3.6 goals above expected while Vladar is below. With a back-to-back-style stretch on the road, how the starts are split, especially against Edmonton, could swing a result.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Flyers' shot share improves against Vancouver and Columbus, the two weaker opponents, or whether they get out-shot even there.

restOfSeason.body:
The 56-point pace overstates the damage because of the opening skid; the last 10 games look more like the real team. Shooting should drift up from 9.2% toward the league norm, and with Woll playing above expected and a solid kill, a points percentage somewhere in the low-to-mid .400s from here is reasonable. That lands this club somewhere around 60 to 72 points, with roughly 24 to 30 wins. It is not a playoff team unless the 5-on-5 share climbs back toward last year's even split.

What won't last: Michkov's finishing rate, and possibly a slice of Woll's goals saved above expected. What could improve: the rest of the forwards' shooting and the young players' share of the minutes. Barkey and Cates are already the only regular forwards winning their minutes. A modest scoring bump to the mid-2s a game is the most likely path, but the team's ceiling stays capped by how often it is pinned in its own zone.
swingFactors: Secondary forwards' shooting warming up as Michkov cools

confidence.note: 19 games; underlying shot share and record agree, though shooting luck is small-sample.
